sections.title: Key takeaways

runs.text: 1) What is aerial bordering?

An extensive programme of surveillance from the sky initiated by European authorities at the EU’s external borders. This platform focuses specifically on aerial surveillance carried out in the Central Mediterranean by Frontex, the EU border control agency, since 2017. This is when, after years of testing, the Agency started to conduct regular aerial patrols through aircraft operated by private companies capable of streaming real-time video.
What does our analysis reveal?

This platform presents the first systematic study of aerial bordering operations in the Central Mediterranean over such an extended period. Due to its scope and use of data collected by the Agency itself, our analysis allows for an assessment of the actual effects of aerial bordering on the ground, beyond institutional narratives and PR strategies. Our analysis shows that:
a.
Frontex’s aerial bordering programme has grown exponentially over the last decade

. This is visible both in the rising amount of money the Agency spends on procuring and testing aerial surveillance services from private contractors (from 11.7€ million in 2018 to 278.6€ million in 2026), and in the increase in the number of hours these planes and drones have been flying in operations over the Central Mediterranean (from 469 hours in 2019 to at least 5253 hours four years later).
b.

Between September 2016 and October 2024, Frontex’s aircraft detected at least 611 migrant boats carrying a total of 33,107 passengers who were intercepted and forcibly returned to Libya or Tunisia. In 2021, the year with the most complete data available,
detection by Frontex’s aircraft accounted for at least 36% of all recorded pushbacks

.  This should be understood as a lower-bound estimate: recently released data suggest that Frontex was in fact responsible for approximately half of all pushbacks. Moreover, while Frontex has refused to share data that would allow us to conduct the same analysis on more recent periods, this data further indicates that this proportion applies also to 2026. Overall, this highlights the
Agency’s continued and significant role in facilitating forced returns
c.
This platform focuses on the role of aerial surveillance in what we refer to as the
“pushback machine”
by highlighting
three key operational patterns

: Frontex’s communication with actors at sea is selective and consistently prioritises the intervention of Libyan and Tunisian authorities over non-governmental rescue groups; Frontex’s aerial operations have resulted in a significant extension of the Libyan Coast Guard’s operational area, including areas well into the Maltese Search and Rescue Zone; and that Frontex aircraft regularly witness direct violence by Libyan and Tunisian actors at sea, yet this has not led the Agency to reconsider its role and activities.
d.

While Frontex has repeatedly maintained that its aerial surveillance programme is employed in the service of rescue, the Agency’s own data, as analysed on this platform, suggests otherwise. In 2021, the year with the most complete data available,
only 5% of operations at sea initiated by a Frontex aircraft sighting led to what, according to current legal standards, can legitimately be defined as rescue

(i.e., when passengers are safely disembarked in Italy or Malta). Beyond search-and-rescue, the Agency characterises its aerial surveillance programme as “multipurpose”, including activities such as “fisheries control.” Our
analysis
reveals that this is a mischaracterisation at best, as
border surveillance activities account for 95% of all events recorded by the Agency itself
You can read more about how we conducted our data analysis in
Methodology
Why is aerial bordering a problem?
Our platform reveals how
aerial surveillance
has become a key component of the EU’s strategy to prevent migrants from reaching Europe by boat and to return them with impunity to violence and abuse in Libya and Tunisia
. More generally, as unpacked in more detail in our
Conclusion

, aerial bordering is at the forefront of some of the most concerning developments in border surveillance across the world: the privatisation of border control; the militarisation of borders; and the collusion with the (Israeli) military-industrial complex.

sections.title: Introduction

runs.text: On 15 June 2017, Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, conducted the first operational flight under its newly established Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance (MAS) service. Following a long testing phase, a surveillance plane equipped with a camera and other sensors live-streamed full motion video and other data from the Central Mediterranean to Frontex headquarters in Warsaw and other coordination centres, where duty officers from multiple European authorities assessed the information.

Operational data collected by Frontex itself and the analysis we provide in this platform show that these flights, which have since become increasingly frequent, are overwhelmingly dedicated to one task: spotting migrant boats to enable their interception and forcible return to Libya and Tunisia in full knowledge of the systemic violence and abuse to which passengers of these boats are subjected in those countries.

The mid-June flight was not the first instance of European authorities flying surveillance missions over the EU’s external borders, and the Central Mediterranean in particular. Since 2013, Frontex has awarded a series of contracts to private contractors to build up its own aerial surveillance programme. Yet the introduction of Frontex’s MAS service in 2017 marks the beginning of a new phase. Whereas border control in the area had previously been predominantly conducted through naval means, aerial patrols have since come to play a primary role. Without these airborne surveillance operations, the Libyan and Tunisian authorities would not be able to intercept migrants at sea and forcibly return them to their shores.

This report identifies aerial bordering as a key development with wide-reaching consequences for the protection of migrants’ rights and for the accountability of state and non-state actors implicated in these abuses. It provides a genealogy of this phenomenon, locating its development within the longer history of European authorities’ attempts to prevent migrant crossings in the Mediterranean regardless of the human cost. The report further explains why aerial surveillance has become so prominent in European border enforcement and why this constitutes a serious human rights issue. In this sense, the report serves as a critical companion to the database section of this platform, allowing readers to contextualise and make sense of the data-driven analysis provided therein.
Chapter 1

examines the interconnected dynamics that underscore the shift in European border control from maritime operations to aerial surveillance–that is, from sea to sky. It is guided by a simple question: what is the problem that aerial surveillance seeks to solve?

Part one charts the retreat of European naval assets and the subsequent near abandonment of search and rescue operations at sea. This retreat was predicated on the simultaneous expansion of Libyan and Tunisian actors’ presence at sea, initiated and made possible through European support. Part two recalls the key developments in this process of “border externalisation” and its disastrous effects on migrants. Part three traces the extraordinary rise of the aerial surveillance regime up to the introduction of MAS and outlines the steps Frontex undertook to establish its systematic aerial presence. Part four examines the targeting and criminalisation of non-governmental aerial monitoring operations.

Overall, the chapter shows that aerial surveillance allows Frontex to closely monitor the Central Mediterranean while avoiding legal obligations to rescue migrants' boats and disembark them to safety in Europe.
Chapter 2
outlines the main characteristics of the current aerial bordering regime since the introduction of Frontex’s MAS service in 2017.

Part one explains how the expansion of Frontex's aerial fleet, through the leasing of manned and unmanned aircraft from private companies, has resulted in a consistent, systematic aerial presence over the Central Mediterranean. It also examines the implications of the ability of Frontex's aircraft to live-stream video and other information to its headquarters and to other European and national authorities, especially concerning decision-making structures and responsibility.

Part two focuses on the role of aerial bordering in what we term the “pushback machine”. It identifies three recurring operational patterns that highlight how aerial bordering underpins interceptions in the Central Mediterranean: first, practices of (selective) communication by Frontex; second, the way aerial bordering expands the operational reach of the Libyan Coast Guard; and third, the routine witnessing by Frontex aircraft of aggressive interception practices by Libyan and Tunisian actors, and how that does not lead to any reconsideration of Frontex’s role in the “pushback machine”. For each of these patterns, a series of exemplary case studies is examined, selected amongst those in the Database based on their relevance and the availability of additional information otherwise absent from Frontex’s own records.
In the
Conclusion

, we situate European aerial surveillance in the Central Mediterranean within the transformation of bordering practices at a global level. Here, we highlight three interconnected phenomena: the privatisation of border control; its militarisation; and its entanglement with the Israeli military-industrial complex.

While several European authorities are involved in the aerial bordering regime, this report focuses on Frontex’s activities. This is not only because the Agency is arguably one of the main actors driving the growing prominence of aerial bordering in the European context, but also because, despite the increasing opacity shrouding its aerial activities, data concerning the activities at sea of the Agency is comparatively more than that of its military counterparts such as national border guards and the European Union Naval Force Mediterranean (EUNAVFOR Med) missions. Further research is needed to examine the role of these other actors.

sections.title: Chapter 1 – The Shift from Sea to Sky (2013–2017)

runs.text: Until recently, the surveillance of the EU’s external borders in the Central Mediterranean was predominantly carried out at sea. Although planes have since long been used as a tool to monitor large swathes of the Mediterranean, their use was relatively sporadic. Instead, maritime vessels were the chosen means of surveillance, enabling European authorities to be physically present over extended periods of time in areas crossed by migrants’ boats and intervene directly by stopping vessels deemed suspicious, destroying empty boats, or deterring so-called “smugglers”.
European authorities have thus always had a strategic interest in maintaining a physical presence at sea. This presence, however, entails a series of legal obligations.

Most notable among these, as enshrined in maritime law, is the duty to rescue people in distress. Moreover, once taken onboard, rescued passengers are protected by various other bodies of law, which oblige ships to disembark rescued migrants in a place of safety, while prohibiting their return to places where their human rights are routinely violated, such as Libya and Tunisia–popular points of departure for migrants. Despite sustained attempts by European authorities to evade these responsibilities, they could not completely ignore them. This created an impasse: how to monitor developments at sea, without becoming implicated in rescue operations resulting in migrants’ safe disembarkation in Europe–an outcome that European politicians have consistently sought to avoid.

The solution was found by shifting surveillance from sea to sky, where such obligations do not apply – or at least not in the same way. While an aircraft pilot remains obliged to notify the relevant authorities of situations of distress at sea, aircraft are limited in their ability to stand by for prolonged periods, let alone embark people in distress.

One thing they can do very efficiently, though, is to spot migrant boats at sea, and inform other ships of their location, in this case those of Libyan and Tunisian authorities, so that the latter can forcibly stop them and return them to their place of departure.

A split along a vertical axis thus ensued: at sea, European authorities have withdrawn much of their naval means, while simultaneously emboldening the presence of their Libyan and Tunisian counterparts to serve as proxies; while in the air, the presence of European aircraft has soared, enabling the early detection of migrant boats, without which Libyan and Tunisian ships would not be able to intercept them.

This chapter unpacks this vertical split, locating this synchronous double movement – the retreat of European assets at sea and the expansion in the sky – within the longer history of European efforts to stop migrants' crossings in the Central Mediterranean.

sections.title: 1. The Retreat of European Authorities at Sea

runs.text: Border control and migrant rescue activities in the Central Mediterranean have changed profoundly over the past few years, with operational zones expanding and contracting and the number and type of naval assets periodically increasing and decreasing. Despite these ebbs and flows, a broader perspective reveals a clear overarching trend of European authorities’ maritime retreat. This retreat has taken place in parallel with active attempts to expel non-governmental organisations that, since 2015, have deployed their own search-and-rescue ships to the Central Mediterranean.

In this section, we argue that, while complex and multi-faceted, this story can be effectively summarised as European authorities’ continuous effort to physically remove themselves and European non-governmental actors from areas at sea where they are most likely to encounter migrant boats. As these dynamics have been the subject of extensive scrutiny by activists, journalists, academics and human rights organisations, they are summarised only briefly here.

sections.title: From Mare Nostrum to Triton

runs.text: The military-humanitarian Mare Nostrum operation, a year-long naval operation focused on rescuing migrants at sea, was launched by the Italian government in the aftermath of the infamous migrant shipwreck of 3 October 2013, in which over 360 people who had departed from Libya lost their lives just a few hundred meters from Italian shores. This shipwreck, followed by an equally tragic one just a week later,
called into question what has been referred to as the “left-to-die” tactics of European authorities.

These strategies, which oscillated between minimal assistance and outright abandonment of migrant boats at sea, had characterised the European response to the surge in migrant crossings that followed the fall of the Tunisian and Libyan regimes in 2011.
Mare Nostrum, despite its problematic “anti-smuggling” rhetoric,
constituted a clear shift away from these tactics.

From the summer of 2014 onwards, the operation became the target of criticism from various political figures over its costs and for allegedly constituting a “pull factor” encouraging more migrant crossings. Although these accusations were subsequently disproven,
Mare Nostrum was terminated in December 2014.

blocks.caption: Map showing the spatial shift from Italian Operation Mare Nostrum to Frontex’ Operation Triton

runs.text: On 1 November 2014, in response to the planned termination of Mare Nostrum, Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard agency, launched operation Triton. In contrast to Mare Nostrum, Triton prioritised border surveillance, not rescue at sea; deploying fewer vessels further away from the Libyan coast.
As later demonstrated,
this retreat formed part of a strategy to deliberately create a “rescue gap” to deter migrants from embarking on the crossing.

Despite this reduced naval presence, Frontex assets were still obliged to respond to Italian Coast Guard requests to carry out rescue operations closer to the Libyan coast. In a confidential letter to the Italian authorities later leaked to the press, the Agency complained about this situation,
suggesting that Frontex viewed the very presence of its ships south of its limited operational area as a potential liability as it exposed them to the rescue obligations enshrined in maritime law.

sections.title: Frontex retreat: from Triton expanded to Themis

runs.text: A shipwreck on 18 April 2015, in which more than 1200 people are believed to have died off the coast of Libya, marked another shift in European authorities’ activities at sea: it forced the EU to admit that “It was a serious mistake to bring the Mare Nostrum operation to an end. It cost human lives.”

and to pledge to extend its maritime presence. In May 2015, Triton’s budget was expanded, its operational area significantly extended southwards (up to 138 nautical miles from Italian coasts), and the number of its vessels and aircraft increased.

Its main operational task, however, remained border control. Fabrice Leggeri, Frontex’s then-director, was quick to declare that: “Triton cannot be a search-and-rescue operation. […] This is not in Frontex’s mandate.”

Although Triton played a limited role in rescues, in the summer of 2017 then-Italian Interior Minister Marco Minniti requested a revision of the operation as part of a coordinated plan to stem migrant arrivals, a plan which also included the criminalisation of non-governmental rescue organisations.
In February 2018, Triton was replaced by a new Frontex operation, Themis.

blocks.caption: Map showing the extend of Frontex Operation Themis

runs.text: One of the main operational shifts in Themis was the pledge that rescued migrants would not be disembarked by default in Italy, as had happened under Triton. The new mission’s operational zone was also decisively shrunk in the Sicily Channel and simultaneously expanded in the Adriatic Sea and south of Sardinia, where rescues have historically been much less frequent. Finally, for the first time in a Frontex mission, Themis included a counter-terrorism security focus,  the “collection of intelligence [to detect] foreign fighters and other terrorist threats at the external borders”.
Operation Themis remains active to this day, yet the number of migrants rescued by Frontex ships remains marginal. Our
data analysis

reveals that across the entire period of 2016 –2023, Frontex initiated only 4.1% of rescues leading to disembarkation in Italy or Malta. Even during recent spikes in migrant arrivals to Italy, such as in 2023, Frontex’s response has been to agree to step up its operations in the sky (doubling aircraft flight hours) and on land (providing “experts” for the registration and identification of migrants in port cities), while only “considering” an increase in patrolling hours for its vessels at sea.

sections.title: EUNAVFOR Med: from Sophia to Dry Sophia and Irini

runs.text: In June 2015, in response to the 18 April shipwreck, the EU launched the anti-smuggling mission of the European Union Naval Force Mediterranean (EUNAVFOR Med), dubbed “Operation Sophia”. In line with European authorities' rhetoric against smugglers, conveniently singled out as the culprits of migrant deaths at sea, the Operation’s mandate focused on anti-smuggling activities, despite the prominence given to rescue activities in public communications.
Spatially, Operation Sophia represented the first significant southward expansion of European presence at sea since Mare Nostrum and aimed to disrupt (migrant) smuggling networks.
While its involvement in rescue operations remained limited compared to other actors,
in absolute terms the number of people assisted by Sophia’s ships was still significant, with “close to 40000 people” rescued until July 2017.

This exposed Sophia to the same critiques that Mare Nostrum had attracted, namely that the operation constituted a “pull factor” leading to more migrants attempting to reach Europe.   This criticism led to two revisions of Sophia’s operational plans,
including the Italian government demanding that rescued migrants no longer be brought to Italian ports by default in July 2017.

Within this tense political context, a key turning point was the “closed ports” policy introduced by the Italian Minister of the Interior Matteo Salvini, who, immediately after taking office in June 2018, began to deny the disembarkation of rescued migrants in Italian ports so as to impose their relocation to other EU member states. To avert the looming possibility of a long standoff with Italian authorities and of “forc[ing] [Libyan authorities] to become the primary actor […] in their area of responsibility”, Sophia’s ships retreated to a “second line” away from Libyan coasts,
and its rescue activities effectively ceased.
In March 2019, all of Sophia’s maritime assets were withdrawn,
leading to the paradox of a “naval mission without any ships”.
One year later, the EU replaced the operation, reportedly referred to by EU policymakers as 'Dry Sophia' during its final year,

with Operation Irini. The decision, triggered by the deteriorating security situation in Libya, involved the redeployment of EU naval assets to the Mediterranean, but in a manner explicitly designed to minimise the “risk” of rescuing migrants.

Irini’s main objective was the implementation of the UN arms embargo on Libya, with the disruption of migrant smuggling networks as a secondary task to be pursued exclusively “through [...] patrolling carried out by aerial assets above the high seas.”
Vessels were deployed only to the north and the east of areas typically crossed by migrant boats,
and the operation included a monitoring mechanism which could trigger a “repositioning clause”, removing vessels from the sea if they were found to generate a “pull factor”.

These operational modalities show how the very presence of ships at sea–even when those ships were deliberately avoiding rescue involvement–was perceived by many European policymakers as a liability to be avoided.

sections.title: Expelling non-governmental organisations from the sea

runs.text: This deliberate process of retreat has gone hand in hand with efforts to expel from the sea the many civil society organisations that, since 2015, have attempted to fill the “rescue gap” left by European authorities by deploying their own ships in the Central Mediterranean. More than 20 non-governmental vessels have taken part in rescue missions in 2025, and several others have been part of this “civil fleet” over the years,
collectively contributing to the rescue of 175,595 people over a decade of operations.

Since late 2016, maritime rescue NGOs have been the target of a sustained campaign of criminalisation orchestrated by several political groups in Italy and beyond. This campaign has attempted not only to smear their reputation by labelling them smugglers, traffickers, and even pirates, and delegitimise their operations through legal action against their crews, but also to effectively drive them out of the sea through administrative and judicial restrictions targeting the most vital asset of every rescue operation: their vessels.

In Italy, the imposition in 2017 of a so-called “Code of Conduct” by then-Interior Minister Marco Minniti, which aimed to severely restrict NGO activity at sea, was followed a year later by Matteo Salvini’s “closed ports” policy. More recently, the 2023 “Decreto Piantedosi” [Piantedosi Decree] has further intensified attempts to restrict and block civilian search-and-rescue activities in the Central Mediterranean. This, combined with the practice of  assigning NGO ships wishing to disembark rescued migrants to ports far away from the area where rescues take place, has forced them into lengthy detours away from their area of operations.
Overall, between August 2017–when the first NGO rescue ship, the
Iuventa

, was impounded in Trapani, Sicily for allegedly participating in human trafficking–and June 2025, European countries (Germany, Italy, Malta, the Netherlands and Spain) have initiated a total of 86 administrative or criminal proceedings against civil search-and-rescue actors.
Although all crews have so far been acquitted of all charges,

demonstrating their unfoundedness, these proceedings have resulted in a significant drain of NGO resources, a breakdown in cooperation among civil society actors, and a noticeable absence of rescue vessels at sea. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, the Piantedosi Decree has led to a cumulative total of 640 days of detention of NGO ships, as well as an additional 735 days spent at sea reaching disembarkation ports deliberately assigned far from rescue areas.

In parallel, NGO vessels have been exposed to increasing violence by the Libyan Coast Guard, including threats, harassment, dangerous manoeuvres and outright attacks. Between 2016 and 2025, 32 such episodes of violence by Libyan actors against NGO vessels, as well as 24 against migrants, three against Italian fishing boats and one against an Italian Coast Guard ship have been documented by the NGO Sea-Watch.
Through these tactics, Libyan actors have directly contributed to efforts to restrict active NGO presence at sea.
Taken together, these elements demonstrate that European authorities’ naval retreat was concurrent with their attempts to expel NGOs from the sea.

sections.title: 2. The Externalisation of Naval Operations to Libyan and Tunisian actors

runs.text: In parallel with the processes of maritime retreat and expulsion outlined above, European authorities have simultaneously worked to embolden Libyan and Tunisian actors’ presence at sea. They have done so with a clear mandate: to stop migrant boats and return their passengers to their point of departure. This process of “border externalisation”, or the outsourcing of border control, allows European authorities to physically prevent migrants from reaching European shores through their proxies, thus circumventing obligations imposed on them by international and national law.
This section provides a brief overview of some of the most significant steps towards the creation of this arrangement which has involved both the provision of
logistical and operational support in the form of vessels, equipment and training
, and the
establishment of a regulatory framework designed to legitimise Libyan and Tunisian interventions at sea

. As denounced by many human rights organisations and search and rescue groups, these combined measures have enabled Italy and other European authorities to institute a regime of “refoulement by proxy”, in which they outsource violence and human rights violations against migrants at sea, while maintaining strategic control from the sky.

The process of border externalisation has been the subject of considerable scrutiny and criticism. Rather than offering an exhaustive account, this section provides a concise overview, focusing specifically on its role in relation to aerial bordering within what we define below as the “pushback machine.”

sections.title: The provision of vessels, equipment and training

runs.text: Externalisation arrangements in the Central Mediterranean initially focused on (re-)building the logistical and operational capacity of Libyan and Tunisian maritime actors, enabling them to serve as naval proxies for the steadily retreating European fleets.
European authorities focused first on Libya, signing cooperation agreements aiming to stem migrant crossings as early as the late 1990s.

In December 2007, Italy pledged to provide the Libyan coast guard with six patrol boats, delivered in May 2009 in the context of an agreement between the two states to conduct joint maritime patrols. This growing collaboration, which was prioritised by European authorities, was interrupted by the fall of the Qaddafi regime in 2011 and the ensuing civil war, which also led to the destruction or damaging of much of the equipment needed by Libyan authorities to conduct maritime patrols, including some of the Italian vessels.
When cooperation with European authorities resumed in 2016, the Libyan Coast Guard was barely functional and “institutionally weak”,
with “limited assets, dysfunctional communication and remote sensing equipment.”

After signing a Memorandum of Understanding with Libya in 2017, Italy stepped up its support by providing the capabilities and equipment needed to stop migrants at sea. Tracking the exact number of vessels supplied to Libya is difficult, due to the multiplicity of actors involved and the opacity shrouding some of the arrangements.

However, Italian investigative outlet IRPI Media found that by December 2022, Italy had supplied and maintained at least 27 vessels for the Libyan General Administration for Coastal Security (7 vessels between 28 and 35 meters long, and about 20 between 9 and 12 meters), and another 17 for the Coast Guard.
At least two additional patrol boats have been donated since.

In addition to these vessels and other technical equipment and support, European authorities have been conducting several training programmes for the Libyan Coast Guard and Navy, in particular through the EUNAVFOR Med operation.

blocks.caption: List of all known vessels donated to Libya by Italy or the EU, Images courtesy of Sea-Watch

runs.text: Similar arrangements have also been made with Tunisia over the last few years, by a larger number of partners. Since 2011, Italy has supplied and maintained at least 12 patrol boats, as well as other equipment and “50 4-wheelers designed to monitor the coasts.”

More recently, Germany provided Tunisia with 12 inflatable boats and 27 boat motors, as well as equipment to repair Coast Guard vessels. In 2023, France announced 25 million euros in aid “enabling Tunisia to buy border policing equipment and train border guards.”
Finally, the EU pledged €150 million towards the “fight against illegal migration” in the context of the Memorandum it signed with Tunisia in 2023.

sections.title: Legitimising Libyan and Tunisian intervention: rescue as legal fiction

runs.text: The provision of logistical and operational support to the Libyan and Tunisian authorities was not sufficient on its own, however. For them to operate with impunity, their interventions at sea had to be made to appear legitimate. This objective has been achieved through the creation of a legal fiction, one where their activities at sea could be presented as “rescues”, rather than as violent interceptions and forced returns to detention and abuse.

Efforts focused initially on Libya and the creation of a Libyan Search and Rescue (SAR) region, the maritime zone within which a state is responsible for coordinating rescue operations. The process of establishing the SAR region began in 2016, when the Italian Coast Guard was instructed by the EU to establish a Libyan Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC), the technical and institutional infrastructure needed to coordinate rescue at sea, and to support the Libyan authorities in “identifying and declaring their Search and Rescue Region".
In 2017, Libyan authorities unilaterally declared a Libyan SAR zone, despite several journalistic investigations revealing that the MRCC was not in operation until at least October 2024.
A similar approach was taken in Tunisia; European authorities have, since 2021, worked to establish a functioning MRCC and to promote the declaration of a Tunisian SAR region.
Various initiatives by European authorities towards the creation of a Tunisian MRCC have been documented.
This process reached its conclusion in June 2024, when Tunisia officially declared its SAR zone.

The declaration creates a legal and operational framework in which Tunisian interceptions of migrants at sea can be framed as rescue, thus shielding the human rights violations associated with them from legal scrutiny.

Over the following years, several actors and groups have challenged the various interconnected elements that sustain the legal fiction of “rescue”. The legitimacy of the Libyan SAR region, which presupposes the presence of a functioning MRCC, and whose declaration needs to follow specific institutional steps, has been contested.

Most rescue NGOs operating in the Central Mediterranean do not recognise the legitimacy of the Libyan authorities, and have consistently denounced and documented their violations including: systematically endangering and directly abusing migrants during operations at sea;
failing to respond to distress calls;
being involved in criminal activities, including high-ranking commanders who have been denounced for human trafficking by the UN;
and threatening NGO and merchant vessels conducting rescue operations  at sea.

Amnesty International and other rights groups have found that the Tunisian coastguard has also repeatedly used dangerous and unlawful tactics during operations that placed individuals at serious risk and led to fatalities.
Reported practices include high-speed manoeuvres producing destabilising waves, physical assault with batons, close-range deployment of tear gas, boat collisions and issuing threats and verbal abuse.
Citing widespread and systematic abuse faced by migrants upon return to these countries, numerous civil society groups, human rights organisations and judges in Italy

have argued that neither Libya nor Tunisia can be considered a “place of safety”, permitting lawful disembarkation following a rescue at sea, nor a “safe third country” to which asylum seekers may lawfully be transferred.

Despite this tireless work of documentation and denunciation, European authorities continue to uphold the legal fiction of rescue, demonstrating its importance in what is referred to below as the “pushback machine”.

In the context of aerial surveillance, Frontex mobilises the legal framework of rescue at sea to justify its policy of communicating the position of migrant boats to the Libyan authorities, whom it identifies as the responsible rescue authority, and whom it therefore claims an obligation to inform. However, this position wilfully disregards not only the documented evidence of abuse that calls into question whether such operations constitute genuine rescues, but also the broader legal obligations binding on the Agency, including the prohibition on returning persons to places where they face persecution or torture.

Within the “pushback machine”, maintaining a veneer of legitimacy around a system documented as producing violence and abuse at scale is what enables Libyan and Tunisian actors to function as European proxies in intercepting people at sea and forcibly returning them to their point of departure.

sections.title: 3. The Rise of Aerial Surveillance

runs.text: The context of European maritime retreat and the simultaneous expansion of Libyan and Tunisian capabilities at sea outlined above sets the scene for the rise of Frontex’s aerial operations. A reduced presence at sea entails a loss of “situational awareness” and the ability to detect migrant boats, particularly in areas close to the North African coast, where migrant boats can more easily be intercepted by Libyan and Tunisian authorities. Instead, by enabling authorities to monitor departing boats while at the same time avoiding the legal rescue obligations held towards migrants, aerial surveillance has come to play a fundamental role in operations.

This section charts the rise of aerial bordering from the sporadic flights of the early 2000s to the establishment by Frontex of a dedicated fleet of aircraft operated by private contractors capable of maintaining a consistent presence over the Central Mediterranean. The following section examines the operational and regulatory shifts that made this transition possible.

sections.title: Building Frontex’s aerial fleet: regulatory changes, new private actors and drones

runs.text: The deployment of aerial assets by European authorities over the Central Mediterranean is not a new phenomenon, but until the introduction of Frontex’s Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance (MAS) service in 2017 airplanes and helicopters were deployed primarily on the basis of specific operational needs during targeted search-and-rescue or surveillance activities. As recalled by a now-retired official of the Italian Coast Guard, the agency that was then primarily responsible for aerial activities, in the early 2000s “air surveillance was not so frequent. [...] We planned our operations precisely in relation to actual SAR situations [....], so I cannot speak of a real, organised air surveillance in relation to migratory flows in those years.”

With the increase in migrant crossings in the Sicily Channel, the situation started to change. As of December 2004, around the same time Frontex was established, the Italian Coast Guard’s Catania Aeronaval Base underwent a significant expansion of infrastructure and fleet, at the time making it one of the most important aerial actors in the Central Mediterranean.

The further rise in sea crossings that followed the so-called Arab Uprisings in 2011 prompted a wider range of actors to rely on aerial assets in their operations. For Frontex, as well as agencies such as the Italian Guardia di Finanza, the Italian Navy, and later the European Union Naval Force Mediterranean (EUNAVFOR Med), aerial surveillance began to play an increasing role in the management of migration in the Central Mediterranean. Joint Operation Hermes, Frontex’s first operation to focus specifically on the Sicily Channel in early 2011, had already deployed a rotating fleet of airplanes, as did its subsequent Joint Operations in the area, Triton and Themis.

During this phase, however, aerial surveillance remained limited. It would take Frontex almost a decade to build its aerial fleet. This development was both a reflection of, and in part driven by, the broader expansion of the Agency's role and activities, during which its budget soared, its tasks multiplied, its cooperation with other EU agencies strengthened, and its personnel expanded.

A series of regulatory shifts and operational tests made the operational debut of Frontex’s key programme, Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance (MAS), possible. A turning point was the introduction of a new Frontex regulation in 2011, establishing that "the Agency may acquire [...] or lease technical equipment for external border control to be deployed during joint operations.”

This proved to be crucial for the implementation of the aerial surveillance programme, as it allowed Frontex for the first time to independently procure its aerial assets without having to rely on the cooperation of EU member states.
After a failed attempt to purchase a surveillance plane to monitor the Greek-Turkey land border in 2013,
the following year Frontex contracted the UK-based company Diamond Executive Aviation (DEA) to provide a fixed-wing aircraft for a 40-day period.

This enabled the Agency not only to assess the “operational effectiveness” and viability of aerial surveillance, but it also, and perhaps most importantly, allowed it to test new practices for carrying out such services.

During this period, the practice of leasing aerial surveillance services from private actors emerged as the “most accessible, qualitative, effective and cost efficient” way of building its aerial fleet, as opposed to the more lengthy and costly option of purchasing its own equipment.
In September 2015, the Agency established its Aerial Surveillance Services (FASS), introducing a framework contract that allowed for the leasing of aircraft for a defined timeframe.

This took place shortly before the European Commission, at the height of the so-called “migration crisis,” proposed the transformation of Frontex into a fully-fledged European Border and Coast Guard Agency, further expanding its mandate, budget, and operational capacities.

As reflected in Frontex’s calls for tenders over the years, 2015 thus marks the beginning of the expansion of the Agency’s aerial fleet through collaboration with private companies. These have included: Vigilance BV and EASP Air BV (both from the Netherlands), DCI (France), MIKC (Latvia), Diamond Executive Aviation (UK) and its Malta-based sister company ESAO Ltd,
Indra Sistemas SA (Spain), and CAE Aviation s.a.r.l. (Luxembourg).

This role of private companies will continue to intensify over the following years.Frontex’s ability to monitor the EU’s maritime borders was also bolstered through collaboration with other EU Agencies such as the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) and the European Fisheries Control Agency (EFCA), with the aim of creating technical synergies in information sharing and surveillance.
In parallel with the use of manned fixed-wing aircraft, Frontex started to deploy unmanned aerial vehicles, more commonly known as drones, several years ago.

Drones have been explicitly indicated by the European Commission as a tool to overcome the challenges of detecting migrant boats across the Mediterranean and have been adopted for maritime surveillance operations by numerous other military actors active in the Central Mediterranean.

The introduction of drone operations required a long series of preparatory steps, beginning as early as 2009.  In addition to training events, demonstrations by manufacturers and technical assessments, significant regulatory changes were needed to allow drone flights in “non-segregated airspace”, i.e., airspace shared by manned and unmanned vehicles.
The first tender for drone testing was issued by Frontex in September 2016 but received no bids.

Test flights began in 2018 after a second call resulting in two contracts: one awarded to Israeli Aerospace Industries (IAI) and Airbus for a drone to be stationed in Crete and operate in the Aegean; and the other to the Italian company Leonardo, which deployed its Falco EVO drone from Lampedusa in the Central Mediterranean.

A third trial was conducted in Portugal in collaboration with the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA), an attempt by the European authorities to involve an agency not primarily dedicated to border enforcement in order to “contribute to a more friendly perception of using this technology”.

Together, these preliminary administrative changes and operational tests paved the way for the beginning of a new phase of aerial bordering at the EU’s external borders–one in which surveillance from the sky, conducted by a consolidated aerial fleet, plays a central role in the forced return of migrants to Libya and Tunisia.

sections.title: 4. Stopping Civilian Aerial Monitoring

runs.text: European authorities are not alone in recognising the crucial importance of aerial monitoring at sea. In parallel with the development of Frontex’s aerial fleet, the Central Mediterranean has also witnessed the emergence of civilian monitoring operations by rescue NGOs, who have sent out their own aircraft to support non-governmental rescue efforts and document human rights violations committed by the authorities themselves.
Non-governmental aerial operations began in 2017, when the NGO Sea-Watch, in partnership with the Humanitarian Pilots Initiative (HPI), launched its inaugural aerial mission with
Moonbird
, a small propeller aircraft.
In 2018, a second NGO aircraft started its operations: the
Colibri
, a reconnaissance plane by the Pilotes Volontaires.
Over the following years, the non-governmental aerial fleet expanded significantly. In 2020, both Sea-Watch and Pilotes Volontaires began operating a second aircraft, the
Seabird 1
and the
Colibri 2
respectively. In 2022, the
Seabird 2
replaced Sea-Watch’s
Moonbird
, while the
Seabird 3
was deployed from 2025, in collaboration with HPI and United4Rescue.
At the end of 2025, the NGO SOS Méditerranée also deployed an aircraft over the central Mediterranean, the
Albatross
, in partnership with HPI.

blocks.caption: Civilian monitoring assets flying in the Central Mediterranean, Images courtesy of Sea-Watch and Pilotes Volontaires

runs.text: Similarly to their maritime counterparts, however, these non-governmental planes have been the subjects of a series of legal and political attacks:
In 2018, Malta blocked Sea-Watch’s
Moonbird
for four months, forcing it to relocate operations to Lampedusa;

In 2019, Moonbird was prevented from operating from Lampedusa for 3 months by the Italian Civil Aviation Authority (ENAC), which argued that Moonbird did not comply with the requirements for its kind of operations.
In 2020, ENAC again grounded
Moonbird
for one month, alleging "spending too many hours at sea and posing a risk of endangering ongoing SAR operations carried out by state actors.”
That same year, Italy contacted Switzerland, where the HPI is based, to argue the aircraft’s operations were commercial and therefore prohibited;

In 2022, Libyan authorities repeatedly denied Sea-Watch entry to their Flight Information Region, the airspace in which flight information is provided, and blocked flight access to the Libyan SAR zone–an act later confirmed to be unlawful by the German Bundestag Research Service;

In 2024, ENAC introduced a new decree threatening aircraft detention and issued five orders banning civilian aerial monitoring from key airports in Sicily, Pantelleria, and Lampedusa. Sea-Watch denounced the flight bans as politically driven: “Italy is trying to get rid of the last witnesses to European crimes in the Mediterranean. We will not be intimidated by this;”
In August 2025, ENAC placed
Seabird 1
under administrative detention with immediate effect, resulting in the first seizure of a Sea-Watch civilian monitoring aircraft.
- In September 2025, Pilotes Volontaires’ aircraft Colirbi 2 was grounded for 20 days.

Taken together, these bans, flight groundings, and bureaucratic obstacles reveal a clear trend: the criminalisation of search-and-rescue NGOs extends also into the air. By restricting their, European authorities can preserve their monopoly over aerial surveillance, thus making it increasingly difficult for civil society actors to document violations in the Central Mediterranean.

sections.title: Chapter 2 – Aerial Operations (2017–2025)

runs.text: Chapter 1 examined how Frontex assembled its vast aerial fleet to patrol the Central Mediterranean. This chapter turns to analysing the Agency’s current aerial bordering regime from 2017 onwards.

During this period, Frontex expanded and consolidated its aerial fleet. After 2017, spending on aerial assets leased privately rose sharply, corresponding to the growth of the Agency's dedicated budget. The amount of money the Agency spends on procuring and testing aerial surveillance services from private contractors went from 11.7€ million in 2018 to 278.6 € million in 2026. The last tender published by the Agency on 25 June 2026 amounts to a staggering 522.6€ million over two years in aerial surveillance services. While it is unclear if, when and to whom a contract has been already awarded in this case, it means that, as of October 2026, the Agency has already allocated 330.9€ million for aerial surveillance for 2027 and 220.3€ million for 2028, sums which are set to continue increasing in the next months.

blocks.caption: Estimated yearly expenditure on aerial surveillance by Frontex.

runs.text: While the Agency does not publicly reveal the identity of the aircraft operating on its behalf at any given moment in time, thanks in part to the investigative work of journalists and non-governmental groups,

LIMINAL was able to compile a list of aerial assets that have been involved in aerial patrols on behalf of the Agency since at least 2019. These include 15 manned aircraft flying out of airports in Malta, Italy and Greece.

In addition, Frontex operates a Heron drone from Malta airport. Manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and operated by ADAS, a subsidiary of the European aerospace giant Airbus, the drone has played a key role in aerial bordering, as described in detail below.

blocks.caption: List of all known Frontex aerial assets flying in the Central Mediterranean between 2018 and 2024

runs.text: This expanding fleet marked a turning point. Through it, Frontex transformed the practice of aerial surveillance from the deployment of targeted operations to an extended presence in the sky–what some have referred to in other contexts as a form of “aerial occupation.”

While this transformation remains an ongoing, continuous process without a clearly defined beginning, we take the introduction of Frontex’s Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance (MAS, sometimes referred to as Maritime Aerial Surveillance) service in 2017 to symbolically mark its start.

sections.title: 1. Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance: Towards Aerial Occupation

runs.text: Frontex describes its Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance service (MAS) as “an integral part of our operations, and a permanent service offered to national authorities. MAS uses surveillance airplanes and drones that stream video and other data from EU and Schengen external borders directly to our headquarters in Warsaw and to national and European authorities, allowing for real-time monitoring.”
MAS was introduced with the stated aim of improving the
“situational awareness”
at EU borders and beyond, and delivering
“a real-time surveillance service”
to Member States and EU agencies.
Below, we unpack those two characteristics to analyse Frontex’s current aerial operations using MAS.

sections.title: Enhanced situational awareness

runs.text: Thanks to its vast fleet, Frontex has been able to increase the consistency of its aerial operations, performing daily take-offs from bases in Malta, Lampedusa or Sicily. This has allowed aerial surveillance over the Central Mediterranean to steadily expand, both temporally and spatially.

From a temporal point of view, Frontex flight time off the coast of Libya and Tunisia has grown remarkably, with aircraft having become a near-constant presence over the last few years. Our analysis of flight data gleaned from aircraft tracking websites and other sources demonstrates this steady increase in global flight time for Frontex aircraft. In our Database, this increase is reflected in the darker blue bars representing daily hours flown by Frontex. Drones in particular have played a key role in this temporal expansion. Frontex’s introduction of drones for aerial bordering has substantially increased the duration and “endurance” of its aerial missions. Our analysis of the collected flight data for the Central Mediterranean reveals that while a surveillance mission by a manned aircraft typically lasts no more than 5,1 hours, a drone’s flight time can reach up to 22,5 hours, with typical missions lasting in average around 11,4 hours.

blocks.caption: Increase of Frontex aerial assets flight hours and Frontex drone flight hours

runs.text: This temporal expansion has also enabled a spatial expansion of the sea areas monitored by Frontex. This means, firstly, that Frontex’s aircraft, and the drone in particular, can monitor areas further away from its bases in Malta, Lampedusa or Sicily, and much closer to North African coasts. The Agency itself has acknowledged that it “has never before patrolled so close to Libyan territorial waters”.

By enabling the detection of migrants’ boats early in their journey, this system has made interceptions by Libyan and Tunisian authorities easier. Secondly, this spatial expansion translates into an increase in the extent and the number of areas patrolled each day. While the Agency does not disclose where its assets patrol, publicly available flight tracking data provide important insights into these aircraft's whereabouts. An analysis of flight tracks of both manned planes and the drone over extended periods of time reveals that each aircraft generally follows a standard search pattern over a designated area of the Central Mediterranean, often for several weeks.
Together, their daily movements constitute a tightly knit, extensive web of aerial patrol.
