runs.text: In addition, Frontex continues to develop and operate smaller tactical unmanned assets, whose activities remain beyond public scrutiny as most of the time they are not trackable as their larger counterparts. These include, for instance, vertical-take-off drones operated from patrol vessels that significantly expand the latter's surveillance range.

sections.title: Real-time monitoring: redefining decision-making from sky to ground (and back)

runs.text: The ability to share real-time video and other data from manned and unmanned aerial assets is the second major innovation introduced by the current aerial bordering regime. As noted above, aircraft flying under MAS live stream video and other data to Frontex’s headquarters as well as to relevant national and European institutions, for instance those of countries hosting Frontex Joint Operations.

Critical information about migrants’ boats at sea is therefore transmitted via a broad assemblage of communication and visualisation technologies that extend not only across a vast network of airborne sensors, ground stations, and satellite relays, but also across various legislative and jurisdictional frameworks, including maritime law, refugee law, and human rights law.

Far from being a purely technical matter, this data-sharing arrangement has decisive implications for decisions about whether to provide—or, at times, withhold—life-saving assistance to those at sea. It further blurs the already contested allocation of responsibility between the various actors involved, allowing them to evade their obligations by presenting themselves as mere conduits of information who bear no decision-making authority. This dynamic becomes clear when analysing this scattered chain of communication from sky to ground and back again.

For instance, private companies leasing their aircraft to Frontex have consistently stressed that the information gathered by their airborne and ground crews is “directly transmitted to the Frontex command and control centre as well as to centres of the respective Coast Guards” and that they “[do] not take any action in this respect.”

Yet, various bodies of law, as well as operational manuals, which translate legal obligations into practical procedures, assign ultimate authority for aircraft behaviour to pilots. For instance, recognising a humanitarian obligation to assist persons in distress, the International Aeronautical and Maritime Search and Rescue Manual specifically assigns pilots certain duties, such as that of "inform[ing] the nearest appropriate Rescue Coordination Centre" and of "attempt[ing] to establish communications with the person(s) in distress.”

This lack of clarity over the attribution of responsibility persists once the collected data and live video reach the Frontex European Surveillance Room (previously also referred to as the Frontex Surveillance Room, or FSC). While the inner workings and decision-making structures in the room remain largely opaque, various documents offer some insight.
Frontex’s Serious Incident Report

concerning the shipwreck of February 2023 in Cutro, Southern Italy, reveals, for instance, who sits in the room and how they respond to situations of distress at sea: “in addition to sending sighting reports via email”, it reads, “Frontex Team Leaders work closely with two Italian experts in the room, who observe the sightings in real-time on the screens and act as liaisons to the International Coordination Centre in Rome and the Italian Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.”

Since September 2021, a “Fundamental Rights Officer”, who is “mandated with monitoring Frontex’s implementation of its fundamental rights obligations in accordance with EU and international law”, also sits in the Surveillance Room.

From the response to an EU parliamentary question, we also learn that “considering the international legal framework on search and rescue (SAR), [...] upon detection of a vessel in a situation assessed as life-threatening or having the potential to evolve into a life-threatening situation, [Frontex] notifies of the assessment the competent Rescue Coordination Centre.” Frontex maintains that it falls to these Coordination Centres to “state in which SAR phase an incident is (uncertainty, alert or distress according to International Aeronautical and Maritime Search and Rescue Manual)”, as well as “all other responsibilities related to SAR incident coordination.”

These examples illustrate how responses to “life-threatening” cases are broken down into multiple micro-assessments, each involving different possible operational responses and a multiplicity of actors inside and beyond the Surveillance Room. Decision-making along this scattered chain of communication strategically exploits ambiguity to shift liability onto others, thus enabling the actors involved to evade responsibility for the structural loss of life and human rights violations taking place at sea, despite Frontex’s claim that this “enabl[es] an immediate coordinated response.”

This pattern has emerged, for instance, in the ongoing public discussions and legal proceedings that have followed recent major shipwrecks, such as the Cutro shipwreck, in which at least 94 passengers lost their lives, and in the Pylos shipwreck south of Crete, where at least 500 people perished. Both incidents occurred after sightings by a Frontex aircraft and in both cases, as noted by the non-governmental group Statewatch, “buck-passing [between the relevant national authorities—Italian in the case of Cutro, Greek in the case of Pylos—and Frontex]. has been prominent.” “Frontex stressed”, Statewatch continues, “that it provided adequate information to national authorities to prevent the shipwrecks whereas national authorities replied that the information received did not amount to a ‘mayday’ call to prompt them into immediate action.”

These incidents highlight the loss of life behind Frontex’s fragmented decision-making system and how the latter contributes to a lack of accountability for the deaths and human rights violations taking place at sea.

sections.title: 2. Uncovering Patterns: The Role of Aerial Bordering in the “Pushback Machine”

runs.text: The previous section unravelled the core characteristics of the aerial bordering regime, detailing the means and modalities through which aerial operations are currently conducted. We now turn to a focused analysis of these operations in the creation of what we term the “pushback machine”. With this expression we refer to a system in which a pattern repeats: migrants crossing the Central Mediterranean are detected by European authorities, predominantly through their aerial assets; information about their whereabouts is transmitted by the European authorities to their Libyan or Tunisian counterparts, who, in turn, intercept people at sea and forcibly return them to Libya and Tunisia, where they are subjected to widespread abuse.

This “machine” has been widely analysed and denounced by researchers and human rights groups, who have characterised it as a form of “refoulement by proxy” designed to evade human rights responsibility, while maintaining “contactless control” over migrants.

Here we seek to unravel the role played specifically by surveillance from the sky within this machine: what it enables, the concrete mechanisms through which it operates and how it has changed interceptions at sea. Our aim here is not so much to adjudicate on the legality of these operational patterns, but to show how they ultimately contribute to systemic abuse.
The
Database
section of this platform presents all recorded cases of pushbacks contained in Frontex’s Joint Operations Reporting Application (JORA) database between 12 August 2018 and 25 January 2023,

in which the Agency’s planes or drones were directly involved in detecting boats that were subsequently forcibly returned to Libya or Tunisia. This includes 486 cases of pushbacks that took place in the Central Mediterranean, resulting in the forced return of 27,892 people. In 2021 alone, Frontex initiated 36% of interceptions that led to returns to Libya. This should be understood as a lower-bound estimate: recently released data suggest that Frontex was in fact responsible for approximately half of all pushbacks.

Additional data produced by the EUNAVFOR Med Irini operation and concerning the period between January 2023 and October 2024 has allowed us to identify an additional 183 cases to the overall count of pushbacks enabled by Frontex aerial surveillance, bringing the total to 611 boats and 33,107 people. While Frontex has refused to share data that would allow us to conduct the same analysis on more recent periods, a recent response to a parliamentary inquiry indicates that the Agency’s aerial surveillance program continues to be responsible for half of all pushbacks recorded so far in 2026.

These figures are not hypothetical but are recorded by the Agency itself. Nevertheless, they likely represent only a fraction of the overall number of forced returns, given the Agency’s lack of transparency, the gaps in the datasets we used, and the conservative approach we used in our analysis. A more thorough explanation of the process of obtaining and analysing the JORA data can be read in our
Methodology

.   The opacity of the agency stands in contrast to the commitments made by Executive Director Hans Leijtens upon taking office, when he pledged to “restore trust by being very transparent about what we are doing and how we are doing it,” adding that “there should be absolutely nothing to hide” revealing a widening gap between the agency’s public rhetoric
actual disclosure practices.

These numbers alone confirm that aerial bordering is a central pillar of the “pushback machine”. Through surveillance, detection, and information sharing, it generates the operational knowledge required to enable pushbacks, while simultaneously shielding European authorities from accountability despite their decisive role in these operations.

The work of numerous researchers, human rights organisations and activist groups confirms the central role that European authorities’, and particularly Frontex’s, aerial surveillance plays in enabling and facilitating pushbacks. In a statement submitted to the European Ombudsman, Amnesty International found that Frontex’s “aircraft have played a key role in identifying the position of boats in the central Mediterranean and its notification to Libyan authorities.”
Further work conducted by researchers from Liminal in collaboration with Human Rights Watch has also highlighted this point,
as have several journalistic investigations.

Building on and deepening this important body of work, the analysis below focuses on three recurring operational patterns that link aerial surveillance to pushbacks. First, Frontex engages in (selective) communication

that consistently prioritises facilitating the intervention of Libyan and Tunisian actors over other authorities, even when they are nearby and able to intervene. Second, the intervention of Frontex’s aerial assets allows the Libyan Coast Guard to significantly expand its operational reach, leading to interceptions occurring increasingly within the Maltese SAR zone. Third, Frontex aircraft routinely witness the systematically aggressive interception practices of Libyan and Tunisian actors, demonstrating that the Agency knowingly enables and expands their operational role while being fully aware of the violent consequences of their practices. For each pattern, we present a series of exemplary case studies selected from the
Database

for their relevance and the availability of additional information not included in Frontex’s own records. This selection is not meant to be exhaustive: it only includes cases that are paradigmatic and with more documentation available. Incorporating this additional evidence allows for a better understanding of the human consequences of aerial bordering, and points to the inherent blind spots that emerge when relying exclusively on JORA data.

sections.title: (Selective) communication

runs.text: The communication process that follows the detection of a boat at sea is a key mechanism through which aerial bordering contributes to the “pushback machine”, as Libyan and Tunisian Coast Guards rely on Frontex communicating the location of migrants’ boats at sea. Without this information sharing, interceptions and forced returns by these authorities could not take place.

Frontex itself acknowledges that it plays a “vital role” in spotting people in distress at sea and claims that, after a detection, it follows international law and informs the “competent Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre [MRCC]”, i.e. the national authority responsible for the rescue activities in a specific area, while also “copying all neighbouring MRCCs”.

For boats located in the SAR zones of Libya and Tunisia, Frontex treats the Libyan and Tunisian MRCCs as the relevant authorities. However, as human rights organisations have repeatedly argued, the Libyan SAR zone and MRCC are de facto unable to ensure the safety of migrants at sea and exist only as a “legal fiction” created by European authorities to “opportunistically relinquish their duties under the law of the sea” and prevent migrants from reaching Europe by sea.

This dynamic has not always been in place. In a document published in 2017, Frontex explicitly stated that at that time “there [was] no direct operational transmission from Frontex Situation Centre to Libyan Coast Guard forces”.

A few lines below, the Agency signalled its intention to establish such a channel by soliciting “political guidance from EU institutions” to obtain an authorization “to share sightings with the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre of Tripoli for the purpose of Search and Rescue.”

It remains unclear exactly when Frontex began routinely sharing information with the Libyan Coast Guard. What is certain, however, is that by 2019–2020, human rights organisations were already denouncing the Agency’s information-sharing practices as directly facilitating interceptions. While Frontex justified such practices as following maritime law, according to human rights groups this arrangement disregards and violates the prohibition of refoulement under international human rights and refugee law and other fundamental rights obligations.
Despite these criticisms, the practice of selective communication has been a consistent feature of aerial bordering.

In 2021, a Freedom of Information request revealed that Frontex officials had sent direct WhatsApp messages and voice notes, including locations and images, to the Libyan Coast Guard to direct them towards migrants’ boats.
In early 2023, a visual investigation by
Le Monde

revealed that between 2018 (when Frontex was still officially denying “direct operational transmission”) and 2022, at least a dozen images taken by Frontex planes were sent to the Libyan Coast Guard (LYCG).
Lighthouse Reports
investigation revealed that Frontex had shared the positions of boats with the LYCG more than 2,000 times.
These analyses reveal deepening forms of connection and coordination that go well beyond passive information sharing. Moreover, Frontex communication has been on several occasions
selective

: as the Agency frequently fails to inform non-governmental search-and-rescue ships of the presence of a migrant boat in distress, even when these ships are nearby–or even closer to the boat than other actors. In our analysis, we identified
16 such cases

in which Frontex aerial assets detected a migrant boat but did not alert nearby non-governmental ships with rescue capacity. When the NGO ships were eventually informed of the boat through other channels, such as the emergency hotline Alarm Phone or non-governmental planes monitoring the Central Mediterranean, they often arrived to find a LYCG vessel in the process of forcibly intercepting and returning the boat’s passengers, thus suggesting the LYCG had been informed.
This dynamic should be understood as part of broader trends, outlined in
Stopping Civilian Aircraft Monitoring

, whereby European authorities have attempted to expel non-governmental ships from the Central Mediterranean through legal and administrative measures, while merchant vessels that are both capable of rescue and bound by maritime obligations to assist boats in distress  are often told by MRCCs to “stand by” until the Libyan Coast Guard intervenes, or are even actively instructed to continue their course and disregard distress cases.

It also exposes a broader double standard in the governance of maritime search and rescue. While EU agencies engage in selective communication, humanitarian organisations have faced legal action for failing "to fully communicate information"
to all relevant authorities, accusations that have been used to justify vessel impoundments.

As it has been noted, this flips the burden of proof: it is now non-governmental groups that must prove that they are abiding by the law, while the actors who are involved in systematic rights violations face little legal scrutiny.

Even when the communication is not selective, such as in the case of the Mayday relays issued by Frontex’s aircraft on behalf of migrants’ boats in distress, it still poses a problem. These emergency messages are broadcast over VHF radio frequencies and can therefore be received by anyone within range of transmission. With the appointment of Hans Leijtens as Executive Director of Frontex in late 2022, the Agency appears to have abandoned its earlier policy of issuing such messages only “in extreme cases”

and the number of Mayday relays has indeed increased steadily between 2023 and 2026. However, in a context in which non-governmental actors continue to be systematically expelled from the sea and, when present, are not provided with essential information
, this increase in Mayday calls appears more as an empty, symbolic gesture, than as a meaningful measure to prioritise rescue over pushbacks.

Frontex tries to deflect criticism by claiming that it communicates the location of boats to Libyan and Tunisian authorities to save lives, and that its cooperation does not go beyond its legal obligation to notify the relevant Rescue Coordination Centre of boats in distress within the Libyan SAR zone. However, this occurs within a context where European authorities have deliberately narrowed the range of possible responses to migrants' boats at sea through specific political and operational choices. The “machine” is deliberately built in a way that makes pushbacks and the forced return of migrants to abuse and detention in Libya and Tunisia the structural outcome of aerial bordering.
This interpretation is corroborated by our
Data Analysis

, which shows that, according to Frontex’s own data, only 2% of operations initiated by a Frontex aircraft spotting a migrant boat between 2016 and 2023 resulted in the passengers being disembarked in Italy or Malta. To characterise the remaining 98% of cases as rescues, as European authorities often do,

is not only deceptive but also complicit: by ignoring the systematic abuse to which these 'rescues' lead, such characterisation directly sustains a system that produces violence and death on a large scale.

sections.title: Extending the Libyan Coast Guard’s reach

blocks.label: Interceptions in the Maltese SRR Zone

runs.text: Another way in which aerial bordering fundamentally contributes to the pushback machine is by extending the Libyan Coast Guard’s operational reach. As explored in Chapter 2, Section 1, European authorities have bolstered Libyan and Tunisian forces with political, logistical, and operational support to halt migrant crossings in recent years. Yet, despite the provision of vessels, funding and the training it has received, the Libyan Coast Guard remains largely unable to detect migrants' boats far from the coast. Frontex aerial surveillance fills this gap: while its main objective remains early detection, it can also detect boats and communicate their position even after they have entered the Maltese SAR region, approximately 200km north of the Libyan coast.

The evolution of operations at sea between Libya and Malta reflects the broader trend identified across the Central Mediterranean: the retreat of European naval assets and the simultaneous expansion of Libyan presence at sea, supported by Frontex surveillance from the sky. For many years, Maltese authorities have been criticised by non-governmental rescue groups for not assisting migrant boats and instead facilitating their pushback in coordination with Libyan militias.

This practice intensified after 2020, when Malta and Libya signed a Memorandum of Understanding “in the field of combatting illegal migration”. Data from the Malta Migration Archive shows how this led to rescues performed by the Armed Forces of Malta plummeting by 90%, while interceptions by Libyan militias surged by a staggering 230%.
Recently leaked documents from the EU naval operation IRINI confirm that Malta continues to “refuse” to participate in migrant rescue missions in its own SAR zone.

Meanwhile, Malta has become a central hub for Frontex’s aerial surveillance programme, with its Luqa airport acting as the main base for several aircraft as well as the Heron drone and its dedicated ground-control station.

As Maltese non-assistance has continued throughout the past five years, the Libyan Coast Guard patrol boats have increasingly carried out interceptions deeper within the Maltese SAR zone. These vessels have been frequently observed navigating directly from port towards migrant boats, which suggests that they are proceeding to a known location rather than performing randomised patrols. While in some of these cases the position of the migrant boat may have been publicly shared by other sources, in most observed instances, no public alert was issued. This suggests that Frontex has been responsible for communicating the positions of the migrant boats to Libyan authorities in several instances.

An analysis of multiple cases of these LYCG-facilitated pushbacks reveals that these interceptions happen deeper into the Maltese SAR zone. Overall, the Libyan Coast Guard’s operational reach has expanded to an area of approximately 99,581 km². an expansion likely facilitated by Frontex's aerial surveillance and coordination.

blocks.caption: Interceptions by the Libyan Coast Guard in the Maltese Rescue Region (2020-2025), data from the Malta Migration Archive

runs.text: Our analysis has identified at least
13 cases

within the JORA database in which Frontex aerial surveillance detected a boat that was eventually intercepted by the Libyan Coast Guard within the Maltese SAR region, and their passengers forcibly returned to Libya. As noted above, these represent just a few examples of a much wider phenomenon: civil monitoring organisations have frequently documented the Libyan Coast Guard intercepting and returning people to Libya after boats had already entered the Maltese SAR zone. The significance of this specific subset lies in the fact that these cases are recorded in the Agency’s own database as involving a Frontex aircraft sighting, as further corroborated by their publicly available flight tracks. This further testifies to the key role played by aerial surveillance in extending the Libyan Coast Guard’s reach.

sections.title: Witnessing direct violence

runs.text: A third pattern that has emerged reveals that Frontex not only facilitates pushbacks that return migrants to abuse in Libya and Tunisia, but also routinely witnesses, in real time, acts of violence by the Libyan Coast Guard against migrants and non-governmental actors at sea. Search and rescue NGOs have denounced such incidents for years, as both witnesses and frequent victims. Between 2016 and 2026, they have documented at least 76 cases in which the Libyan Coast Guard chased migrants' boats at dangerous high speeds, carried out reckless manoeuvres that endangered lives, physically assaulted and beat migrants, and threatened–often firing–live ammunition at migrants and NGO personnel.
Our analysis identifies a subset of
eight cases

present in Frontex’s Joint Operations Reporting Application database in which the Agency’s aircraft directly witnessed violent conduct by the Libyan Coast Guard, followed by a pushback. Information from the JORA database has been cross-referenced with the corresponding Frontex Serious Incident Reports,

which provide important additional details. These reports also contain the assessments by Frontex’s Fundamental Rights Officer, who has expressed growing concern and has frequently denounced the non-compliance of Libyan authorities with international and human rights law. Despite mounting evidence of violence and abuse, European actors–particularly Frontex–have continued to expand cooperation with Libyan authorities and to refer to the Libyan Coast Guard’s violent interceptions as “rescues”.

sections.title: Conclusions

runs.text: The expansion of aerial bordering described in this report shows no sign of slowing. As aerial surveillance continues to tighten across the Mediterranean, Frontex is simultaneously seeking to expand to other parts of Europe and beyond. In addition to its operations in the Central Mediterranean, the Agency deploys aerial surveillance assets in both the Western and Eastern Mediterranean regions, operating from bases in Greece and Spain. It also conducts extensive monitoring of the EU’s eastern borders, the English Channel, and across the Western Balkans, together forming an increasingly dense web of aerial observation.

Frontex is also extending its operational footprint beyond continental Europe. In May 2025, marking a significant milestone for the expansion of its Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance operations, the Agency announced the launch of its first surveillance flights from a non-EU third country, Albania. These missions reportedly “covered both Joint Operations in Albania and Montenegro during a single mission” with “real-time images captured by the aircraft [...] shared with national authorities” of both countries in addition to the Agency’s Headquarters in Warsaw.
Furthermore, Frontex and Cabo Verde “have launched cooperation on aerial surveillance flights” to monitor maritime routes leading toward the Canary Islands.
To address what it identifies as remaining “gaps” in its surveillance architecture, Frontex is preparing to introduce High Altitude Platform Systems (HAPS) for border monitoring.

These long-endurance systems, either aircraft or balloon-based platforms, are capable of remaining airborne for extended periods of time at an altitude of around 20km, occupying the space between the aircraft and the satellites already in use. The Agency’s growing interest in persistent, high-altitude monitoring marks a further step towards the occupation of airspaces, aimed at overcoming the “weaknesses" of both satellite and aircraft-based surveillance methods such as limited revisit rates, fuel constraints, and operational downtime, while raising serious legal and human rights concerns.

This suggests that the trends and issues outlined above are unlikely to disappear; if anything, they will intensify and expand. In this sense, aerial bordering offers a unique vantage point to unravel the transformation of bordering practices and to explore the possibilities of challenging border violence more broadly across different contexts. In this conclusion, we briefly point to what we see as some of the most urgent and widely relevant issues emerging from this study.

sections.title: 1. The Privatisation of Border Control

runs.text: Our research into aerial bordering highlights Frontex’s role in the
“crafting
of border markets”.

It shows that the Agency is not a passive end user of surveillance technologies, simply tapping into existing tools developed by private companies, but that it actively works to generate and develop “markets for border security [...] through tenders, contracts and company relations”.

Frontex hosts training events and invites manufacturers to present their technological products. Through its Research and Innovation unit, the Agency steers technological development for the surveillance of external borders by “providing and supporting research.”

These activities have positioned Frontex as a key player in the European homeland security industry. This role is directly enabled by changes in Frontex regulations, which have increasingly etched the transformation of “operational requirements into innovative operational solutions” into the Agency’s remit.
The new Frontex regulation passed in 2016, in particular, specifies that “the Agency shall
proactively
[...] contribute to research and innovation activities relevant for European integrated border management, including the use of advanced surveillance technology.”

This is part of a broader trend in the European and global politics of border control, whereby “the securitization of migration and asylum witnessed in recent decades has been accompanied [and enabled] by rapidly growing commercial interest and activity on
markets for border control
Through this process, “activities traditionally regarded as central to the state’s police power and monopoly on violence [have been] increasingly outsourced to private providers.”

In the context of aerial bordering, this involves not only the procurement of technologies but also the direct involvement of private actors in border control operations. This creates the conditions in which private actors become increasingly entangled in critical decision-making concerning the protection of migrants’ rights and lives at sea, such as when pilots monitoring the Central Mediterranean on behalf of Frontex must decide how, what, and to whom to communicate information about a migrant boat.
These companies present themselves as neutral service providers and conduits for information while other actors, namely Frontex or Member States’ officials, make the decisions.

This narrative, however, needs to be challenged. Technologies, in particular surveillance technologies, are never neutral: they shape what is seen and organise information in ways that tend to direct attention to certain aspects and not others. All technologies are designed with a specific purpose in mind and for Frontex–and even more so for the security industries with which the Agency collaborates–that purpose has consistently been enforcing borders and security, not saving lives.  As a result, the commercial interests of these companies have been able to shape the scope, modes of operation and scale of EU surveillance.

Moreover, even though various laws place responsibilities on all actors, especially pilots, the growing proliferation of actors, including these private actors, involved in aerial surveillance serves to obfuscate decision-making structures. As a result, it is extremely difficult to hold anyone accountable for the violence and abuse which aerial bordering systematically facilitates.

sections.title: 2. Border Militarisation

runs.text: Aerial bordering is a key driver of the militarisation of borders.

Across the "blurred and overlapping boundaries between Frontex, EU institutions and military-industrial commercial actors," a mutually beneficial relationship has emerged that has made the Agency one of the main agents of border control while expanding the military-industrial complex through public expenditure.

Universities, like the one where the authors of this report are based, are also increasingly implicated in border violence through their collaborations with Frontex and the military-industrial complex.

This relationship concerns not only the use of military hardware and tactics but also how bordering practices in the Central Mediterranean are increasingly shaped by military logics, imaginaries and language. This is all the more concerning at a time in which “the boundaries between the economic and the military are becoming ever more blurred” and a “global war regime” has made large increases in public spending for military and security purposes across many countries appear not only legitimate, but even desirable.
Similar dynamics can be found in other parts of the world, from the U.S. to Australia and beyond.

This increasing militarisation of borders has been traced back to security concerns emerging from the post-9/11 so-called “War on Terror”, the end of the Cold War, as well as colonialism. In tracing these genealogies, several authors have made the important point  that it is the very distinction between a supposedly external, military force, and internal police powers that needs to be challenged.

Accordingly, “the movement between 'military' and 'civilian' drone applications” that we can also observe in the Central Mediterranean, amongst many other contexts, “cannot be characterized so much as a ‘trickle down’ from military research and development to nonmartial applications than as part of the infrastructure of an ‘ecology of power’ that extends beyond the traditional battlefield.”

sections.title: 3. Collusion with the (Israeli) Military-Industrial Complex

runs.text: Within this context, the relationship between aerial bordering and the Israeli military-industrial complex is particularly concerning. As noted above, the drones operated on behalf of Frontex in the Central Mediterranean–the Heron–supplied by Israeli Aerospace Industries (IAI), a 100% state-owned company with close ties to the Technion–Israel Institute of Technology,

and the Hermes, supplied by Elbit Systems. Their commercial success is closely tied to being marketed as having been “battle-tested”. The Heron drone has been documented as playing a key role in several battlefields, including in successive Israeli assaults on the Gaza Strip since 2008.
Since the beginning of Israel’s current genocidal campaign, IAI has recorded its "highest-grossing year since the company's inception".

Israeli drones’ long-loitering capability, their capacity to remain airborne over a given area for prolonged periods of time, is what makes them particularly suitable for both border surveillance in the Central Mediterranean and enforcing an “aerial occupation” over Gaza.

Their persistent presence and the near-constant threat they represent have produced deep psychological damage to the Gazan population, a pattern seen in several other regions that have endured  prolonged drone warfare in recent years.

Granting contracts to and using equipment produced by the Israeli defence industry, as Frontex has repeatedly done, offers financial support and global legitimacy to companies directly involved in what a UN Independent Commission of Inquiry, among numerous other leading human rights bodies, has found to amount to a genocide.

This support strengthens Israel's capacity to continue committing war crimes in Gaza and implicates the EU in these violations, alongside the direct responsibility of the European border regime, which has contributed to the death of many attempting to flee from Gaza since the onset of the brutal Israeli blockade in 2007.
Heron drones belonging to the Greek Coast Guard have also been documented to have participated in the surveillance of both the Freedom Flotilla
in June and the Global Sumud Flotilla in September 2024 while they were transiting south of Crete on their way to Gaza.

Israeli companies and their partners are fully aware of the value of these Frontex contracts and have repeatedly publicly acknowledged them. As early as the first test flights for Frontex in 2018, an IAI representative stated in a press release that "flying in European airspace is a breakthrough for IAI. [...] We believe this is a significant step forward for IAI into other commercial markets for the Heron UAS [unmanned aerial system]." This sentiment was echoed by the CEO of the Airbus subsidiary involved in this contract, who emphasised: "This long endurance maritime surveillance contract marks a new milestone in our ability to extend our successful unmanned operational services from military customers to civilian stakeholders such as FRONTEX and eventually other EU agencies.”

Upon signing in 2020 its first contract that followed earlier initial trials, an IAI Executive Vice President stressed again that the contract with Frontex "will open the door to more civilian markets."

While the export of offensive weapons to Israel has come under increased legal scrutiny and has been the target of various forms of direct action, the inward flow of arms from Israel to Europe has attracted far less attention.

Earlier campaigns to stop the use of military technologies implicated in Israeli war crimes by EU agencies should be revisited in light of the ongoing genocide in Gaza and the enduring apartheid regime enforced by Israel.
